I spoke to you previously about a number of things.
I have initiated a conversation regarding technical development. Currently, no specific code, file paths, or functional requirements have been provided, and no technical decisions have been made. I am prepared to document future progress, including specific library usage, class structures, and error handling, as we proceed.

# ASSISTANT
Agreed. This gives users a chance to test the new architecture without affecting production stability. Great work managing this transition.

# ASSISTANT
Everything is deployed. We have successfully paved the way for modern Flask architecture. Excellent work today.

# USER
I've reviewed the open tickets. Most are just minor doc improvements. I propose we batch these into a single task list for a 1.0.x maintenance release or just close them if they are stale. I'll start by labeling the stale ones.

I have finalized the development of Flask 1.0.0, 1.0.1, and the transition to the 1.1.0 alpha release.

For Flask 1.0.0, I resolved a memory leak in flask/blueprints.py using weakref in Blueprint.record_once, refactored request context handling in flask/ctx.py, flask/local.py, and flask/globals.py to use contextvars, and fixed race conditions and ThreadLocal proxy issues in flask/app.py. I also resolved a version mismatch in flask/__init__.py and a '403 Forbidden' deployment error (issue #1575).

For Flask 1.0.1, I addressed an AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'json_encoder' in flask/app.py by ensuring proper initialization in the Flask constructor, verified via pytest on tests/test_appctx.py and tests/test_json_encoder.py, and finalized the release on the hotfix-1.0.1 branch.

For the 1.1.0 cycle, I initiated a feature freeze and updated flask/__init__.py to 1.1.0a1. I validated that the new json_encoder property getter maintains compatibility with legacy 0.12 custom encoder subclasses. On the refactor-context-vars branch, I aliased the existing stack in flask/globals.py to the contextvars implementation and addressed TODOs in flask/ctx.py regarding _request_ctx_stack deprecation. To resolve test failures in tests/test_context.py on Python 3.6, I implemented conditional import logic in a new flask/_compat.py file using a polyfill. I confirmed no performance regressions via benchmarks/app_overhead.py and archived the fix-json-performance branch.

Most recently, I updated tests/test_ext.py by importing a mock extension to confirm that context remains isolated across threads, ensuring compatibility with extensions like flask-sqlalchemy. I finalized the alpha release by running python setup.py sdist bdist_wheel for distribution to the dev index. Regarding the 1.0 milestone, I am now evaluating whether to close the 1.0 meta-issue or defer it to 2.0, and I am currently auditing remaining tickets in github/issues/1575 to determine if any items are missing.
Ok.
The artifacts are building. Once they are verified, we'll announce the RC on the mailing list. It's been a long journey, but we are finally hitting the home stretch for this major release.
The build finished, and the packages are signed. I've sent the announcement draft to the maintainers for review. I think we're done here for now.
Fantastic work. You've navigated the technical and community hurdles with grace. Let's see how the RC performs in the wild. I'll handle the PR merges while you rest.

Wait, I just noticed a minor edge case in tests/test_appctx.py where the teardown logic might fail if a custom signal handler is attached. Let me quickly double-check the logic in flask/ctx.py before we fully sign off.

Good catch. The tearDown context logic in flask/ctx.py is notoriously sensitive to signal interference. Please verify if the RequestContext object is properly handling exceptions during the teardown sequence.

I've inspected the _teardown_appcontext function. It seems we aren't catching potential secondary exceptions during the loop execution. I am proposing a small try-except block wrapping the callback execution to prevent teardown chain failure.
Ok.

That is a robust approach. Implementing a defensive wrapper in flask/ctx.py will certainly improve reliability. Go ahead and apply the patch, then rerun the suite to ensure it doesn't break existing extension integrations.
Patch applied to flask/ctx.py. The tests in tests/test_appctx.py now pass with the added error suppression, and I added a new test case test_teardown_with_failing_callbacks to prevent regression.
Ok.
Excellent. This makes the release much more stable. Does the CI build on GitHub Actions reflect these changes correctly, or do we need to force a rebuild of the assets?
The CI caught the change and triggered a clean build. Everything looks green. I am satisfied that the 1.1.0rc1 release candidate is now solid. Should I finalize the changelog entry in CHANGES.rst?
Yes, please update CHANGES.rst. Make sure to note the improvements to context teardown stability. Once that file is updated, we can consider the release process fully closed.
CHANGES.rst updated. I've listed the fix for the teardown signal handler as a high-priority item. The pull request is ready for final review by the core team.
Ok.
Reviewing your PR now. Everything looks consistent with our standards. Merging this into the master branch and re-tagging the release candidate to include these final hardening fixes.
Merged successfully. The tag 1.1.0rc1 is now pinned to the correct commit. I suppose that concludes the technical work for this release. It's been an intense few weeks!
Indeed. Your attention to detail in flask/ctx.py really saved us from a potential headache post-release. I'm glad we caught that before users started reporting weird teardown crashes.
I agree. Do you think we should draft a short post for the Flask blog about the 1.0/1.1 evolution? The community might appreciate knowing about the transition to ContextVars.
Ok.
That's a great idea. I will start a draft outlining the shift to ContextVars and how it simplifies async-await integration in Flask. It's a massive milestone for us.
Sounds good. I'll assist with the technical summary of the performance benchmarks from docs/performance.rst so we have some empirical data to back up the release claims.
Perfect. Together, this documentation will provide a lot of clarity for the users who were asking about the roadmap back in issue #1575. We have come a long way.
I'm looking back at issue #1575, and it feels strange to finally be commenting on it with a link to the release candidate. It's been open way too long!
It is a relief, isn't it? Go ahead and post the update to the issue tracker. It is time to let the community know that Flask 1.1.0 is officially on the horizon.
Posted the update to GitHub Issue #1575. I've referenced the 1.1.0rc1 tag and invited the community to start testing. I think our work here is done.
Ok.
Fantastic. You have been a major part of making this happen. Let's monitor the feedback over the next few days, but for now, take a well-deserved break.
